title: Rita Wilson Says She’s Returning for Lena Dunham’s ‘Girls’ Revival: ‘I Would Do Anything for Her’
description: Evie Michaels is back! Rita Wilson is teasing plans to reprise her “Girls” role as Marnie Michael’s eccentric mother in Lena Dunham’s much-anticipa
body:
Evie Michaels is back! Rita Wilson is teasing plans to reprise her “Girls” role as Marnie Michael’s eccentric mother in Lena Dunham’s much-anticipated revival.

	When asked by People if she’ll be returning for the new iteration of the hit show, Wilson told the publication, “That is what I’m hearing, so I don’t think Lena would be lying about that.” The actress went on to say that she is “so excited” about the series return, Wilson first joined the show during Season 2 and made guest appearances throughout the show’s run. 
	

	“Oh my gosh, yes. I mean, Lena is one of the most talented people I’ve ever worked with. I would do anything for her,” she continued. “I would bend over backward. And then I love Allison Williams who, you know, I was lucky enough to play her mom.” She added: “I know Lena’s gotta be cooking up something very good.”


	Earlier this month, it was announced that HBO had greenlit a revival of “Girls,” the dramedy created by Dunham. The series will return for a limited, five-episode run with production beginning in 2027 — a decade after the Season 6 finale.

	With Dunham as creator, showrunner and star, the original series ran from 2012 to 2017 and followed a group of friends through the misery and dysfunction of their 20s in New York City. All four core cast members are returning for the revival: Dunham as Hannah Horvath, Allison Williams as Marnie Michaels, Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro. Additionally, Andrew Rannells reprises the role of Elijah Krantz.

	Wilson first joined the show during Season 2 and made guest appearances throughout the show’s run. 
	

	Judd Apatow returns as executive producer on behalf of Apatow Productions alongside Dunham, Ilene S. Landress and Michael P. Cohen of Dunham’s Good Thing Going banner. Williams, Kirke, Mamet and Rannells serve as co-executive producers.

schema.headline: Rita Wilson Says She’s Returning for Lena Dunham’s ‘Girls’ Revival: ‘I Would Do Anything for Her’

title: Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83
description: Bob Buziak, former president of both RCA Records and Sony’s TriStar Music Group, died on October 19, a rep confirms to Variety. No cause of death w
body:
Bob Buziak, former president of both RCA Records and Sony’s TriStar Music Group, died on October 19, a rep confirms to Variety. No cause of death was announced; he was 83.

	Buziak was best known for reviving RCA’s fortunes in the 1980s with hit albums by Bruce Hornsby, Eurythmics and Love and Rockets, not to mention the blockbuster soundtracks to the “Dirty Dancing” films, which spawned a No. 1 single with Eric Carmen’s “Hungry Eyes” and an Oscar- and Grammy-winner with Bill Medley and Jennifer Warnes’ “(I’ve Had) The Time of My Life.”
	

	He left a job at the Ford Motor Company in 1968 to work in the music business, taking on distribution and promotion roles in Detroit and San Francisco before joining Capitol/EMI Records in Los Angeles. He held promotion and A&R roles at that label before joining Arista Records, where he thrived as head of West Coast operations and, later, managing director in the U.K. His performance at that label led directly to his being named president of RCA in 1986.


	While there, Buziak’s distribution deals with indie labels like Beggars Banquet (which brought Love and Rockets and others) and Jive helped expand and modernize the label’s roster.

	He left the label in 1990 to serve as president of Sony’s TriStar Music Group and later founded Chameleon Entertainment as a joint venture with Time Warner. In 1995, he launched Buziak & Company LLC, which consulted for telecom and cable companies, and played a key role in the sale of Paradigm Music Entertainment to Liberty Media.

	He was a board member of inVentures a U.K. investment group and initiated a merger with Redwood Partners a U.S. corporate search firm to create a multi-platform international consulting and venture group.

schema.headline: Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83

title: Role Model Shouts Out Jake Shane and Renee Rapp, Channels Chuck Timely on Final North American Tour Date: Concert Report
description: Without stretching the metaphor too far, Chuck Timely’s hourglass was closer to running out than he might have thought: While the second of two Lo
body:
Without stretching the metaphor too far, Chuck Timely’s hourglass was closer to running out than he might have thought: While the second of two Los Angeles dates of Role Model’s “Chuck on Tour” jaunt in support of his third studio album — titled (naturally enough) “Chuck Timely & the Hourglass” — was scheduled to be the second-to-last North American show, it actually was the last, as he canceled the next night’s final stop in Berkeley due to illness.
	

	However, there was no sign of illness at the Greek Theatre on Friday night, as Role Model took the stage in his latest persona, the time-traveler Chuck Timely. (He was the Saint Laurent Cowboy for his 2024 album “Kansas Anymore.”) He has described his new character as someone who’s “been around through all the eras and seems to grab little pieces from each along the way. He’s been around forever.”

	The show started on a slightly awkward note, as Role Model made a grand entrance to a pre-recorded “Chuck’s Mantra,” emerging from the darkness for “High Hopes 3000.” But when the track dropped out for a few moments, a confused silence overtook the 6,000-strong audience. And when the track finally resumed, the lyrics were nearly drowned out by the eruption of cheers as Pillsbury’s silhouette was illuminated by golden lights.


	With that, the energy kicked in. “I don’t say this every night, and I didn’t say it last night,” he shouted, “but you can tell when a show is going to be fucking lit one song in — and tonight’s going to be a fun night!”

	Pillsbury maintained the energy throughout his 90-minute set, alternating between singing and playing acoustic and electric guitars, with the energy only slowing down for lower-key songs like “The Longest Goodbye” and “Good Thing,” the latter of which inspired hundreds of fans to wave their phone flashlights.
	

	The stage set was kept simple, with comical placements cards for each of the bandmembers, including “Bass God,” “Piano Man” and, of course, “Chuck,” while a marker at the back of the stage read, “Stand here for the drama.”

	Though he didn’t stand in the designated spot, Pillsbury reminded the audience of the drama surrounding his track “Love I You,” which features his now-ex Dakota Johnson. Rather than use Johnson’s voice during the live performance, Pillsbury invites someone from the audience each night to recite the song’s popular back-and-forth.

	But the setlist dipped into Role Model’s pre-Chuck eras, including “Writing’s on the Wall,” “Slipfast,” “Old Recliners” and, of course, the evening’s most-anticipated song, “Sally, When the Wine Runs Out.”

	The night also had, as he put it, “some tea”: not only were Role Model’s parents in the house, but he also said that his friend, online personality Jake Shane, had attended Thursday night’s show because he knew singer Reneé Rapp would be at Friday’s.

	“He wanted all the fucking attention on him, so he decided to come last night because he knew Reneé would take all the attention from him,” Pillsbury told the crowd. “And that’s fucking true!”

	As the audience erupted in cheers and scanned the crowd for Rapp, Pillsbury said, “Alright stop looking at her, look at me,” he laughed. “I got fucking dressed up for you.”

schema.headline: Role Model Shouts Out Jake Shane and Renee Rapp, Channels Chuck Timely on Final North American Tour Date: Concert Report

title: Kris Bowers Set to Compose Original Score For Disney’s Animated Feature ‘Hexed’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Academy Award winning composer Kris Bowers is set to score the music for the upcoming Disney animated feature “Hexed.”

	The film stars Hailee Stei
body:
Academy Award winning composer Kris Bowers is set to score the music for the upcoming Disney animated feature “Hexed.”

	The film stars Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones, Jodie Foster and Walton Goggins in a magical coming-of-age saga. “Hexed” follows an unconventional teenage girl who discovers secret magical abilities which, once unleashed, hurtle her into a spectacle-filled journey through a hidden realm of witches.


	“Hexed” is set to hit theaters on Nov. 25.
	

	Bowers said, “Creating the score for ‘Hexed’ was all about exploration and experimentation. Inspired by a young woman who dreams of flying, both literally and metaphorically, I began exploring unusual ways of making music with air: bird call whistles, wind wand, nose flutes, bottles, kazoos, air sirens and even recordings of actual birds transformed into instruments.” He added, “The film’s unique take on a magical realm inspired a sound that blends orchestra, an effected chamber woodwind ensemble, synths and natural sound elements, often blurring the line between acoustic and electronic textures. At its core, this is a deeply emotional mother-daughter journey and I wanted the music to capture both that intimacy and the wonder and adventure of this world. I’m so grateful for the incredibly engaging collaboration with Fawn, Jason, Jared and the entire Disney Animation filmmaking team.”

	Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand direct the film, with Roy Conli and Yvett Merino on board as producers.

	In addition to scoring “Hexed,” Bowers also composed the music for Netflix’s animated film “Steps.” Additionally, he scored the upcoming Paramount/Skydance sports drama, “Mr. Irrelevant: The John Tuggle Story, which premieres on Dec. 25.
	

	Bowers will also reunite with filmmaker Ben Proudfoot. He composed the score for Breakwater Studios’ documentary “The Eyes Of Ghana.”

schema.headline: Kris Bowers Set to Compose Original Score For Disney’s Animated Feature ‘Hexed’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Hunter Schafer Reveals She Had Gender-Affirming Bottom Surgery
description:
Hunter Schafer has undergone bottom surgery, the “Euphoria” star revealed.

	“I just had bottom surgery in December, which was amazing, and I love
body:
Hunter Schafer has undergone bottom surgery, the “Euphoria” star revealed.

	“I just had bottom surgery in December, which was amazing, and I love it so much,” Schafer told Elle magazine, referring to the gender-affirming operation that alters a person’s genitals to align with their gender identity.

	“For a long time I’ve embraced the gender-expansive part of myself, and I really wanted to try to make that previous body work, because I thought there was something really cool and badass about it,” she said. But, according to Elle, Schafer described “hitting a wall again and again where this theoretical queer utopia didn’t match up with the world she encountered every day, and the way she personally wanted to show up in it.” And so while every trans person is different, a medical transition was the right decision for Schafer.
	

	Schafer described that ability to evolve as the “magical thing about queerness” — that “on an ideological level, it’s about possibility and expansion and growth, and being on that journey and finding yourself.” While she had always viewed her gender identity as more fluid, she has now landed somewhere “flatter,” she described. “I’m a woman. I’m a girl,” she said. Coming to that conclusion required Schafer to wrestle with queerness as a philosophy “versus how it applies and works in real life, in the context of the world that we’re living in.” She said, “I feel like there’s always a tension there.”

	Schafer described her recovery from bottom surgery in early 2026, noting that she rented a big apartment and had friends and family visit while she was required to lie flat. “I think my limit was 150 steps per day, which is nothing,” she said of her doctor’s orders.
	

	Schafer, who will next be seen opposite Michelle Yeoh in the Amazon miniseries “Blade Runner 2099,” spoke a couple of years ago about not wanting her identity to overshadow her work, saying she herself had tried to avoid saying the word “trans” during interviews. “It has not just happened naturally by any means. If I let it happen, it would still be giving ‘Transsexual Actress’ before every article ever,” Schafer told GQ in 2024.

	“As soon as I say it, it gets blastoff,” she added about when the word “trans” comes up in her interviews. “It took a while to learn that and it also took a while to learn that I don’t want to be [reduced to] that, and I find it ultimately demeaning to me and what I want to do. Especially after high school, I was sick of talking about it. I worked so hard to get to where I am, past these really hard points in my transition, and now I just want to be a girl and finally move on.”

	Schafer acknowledged in that interview that “it’s a privilege” to be able to shift focus beyond her gender identity, saying: “It’s been very intentional. I’ve gotten offered tons of trans roles, and I just don’t want to do it. I don’t want to talk about it.”

	“I know for a fact that I’m one of the most famous trans people in media right now, and I do feel a sense of responsibility, and maybe a little bit of guilt, for not being more of a spokesperson,” Schafer concluded. “But ultimately, I really do believe that not making it the centerpiece to what I’m doing will allow me to get further. And I think getting further and doing awesome shit, in the interest of ‘the movement,’ will be way more helpful than talking about it all the time.”

	Schafer’s first acting rule was Jules in the HBO smash hit “Euphoria,” which made her a celebrity — and a role model for trans people — in her early 20s. Her other roles include “The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” and the Neon horror movie “Cuckoo.”

schema.headline: Hunter Schafer Reveals She Had Gender-Affirming Bottom Surgery

title: Fox Corp. Top Lawyer Adam Ciongoli Is Exiting, Nick Trutanich to Take Over as General Counsel
description: Fox Corp. said Adam Ciongoli, chief legal and policy officer, will not renew his contract — and that he will step down from the role effective Dec.
body:
Fox Corp. said Adam Ciongoli, chief legal and policy officer, will not renew his contract — and that he will step down from the role effective Dec. 1. Ciongoli will serve as a special adviser to Fox through June 2028.

	Nicholas Trutanich, currently Fox Corp.’s executive vice president, principal deputy general counsel, will become general counsel of the company with Ciongoli stepping down. Trutanich will report directly to executive chair and CEO Lachlan Murdoch.
	

	The changeover comes as Fox Corp.’s $22 billion deal to buy streaming-platform company Roku remains pending. The companies expect the deal to close in the first half of 2027. Shareholders of both Fox and Roku approved the agreement, which is still pending Justice Department clearance.


	Before joining Fox in 2023, Ciongoli was general counsel and chief sustainability, corporate responsibility and governance officer for Campbell Soup Co. He previously was general counsel of Lincoln Financial Group, Willis Group Holdings PLC and Time Warner Europe. Before moving into the private sector, Ciongoli served as counselor to John Ashcroft when he was U.S. attorney general; as chief counsel to the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on the Constitution, Federalism and Property Rights; and as law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.

	“I’d like to thank Adam for his many immense contributions over the last three years,” Lachlan Murdoch said in a prepared statement. “I deeply appreciate his service to Fox and am grateful that he will continue to serve Fox as a special adviser. Nick Trutanich has been a critical member of the Fox team since joining the company five years ago and will bring deep legal, litigation and compliance experience to this expanded role.”
	

	Ciongoli, in a statement provided by Fox Corp., said: “It has been a privilege and an honor to be a part of the Fox family, and I have especially valued my relationships with Lachlan and our talented colleagues. I look forward to continuing to work with Lachlan and Fox as a special advisor to help this great company in its continued successes.”

	Prior to joining Fox, Trutanich served as the U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada from 2019-21 and previously held senior roles at the Nevada attorney general’s office and served as a federal prosecutor within the DOJ. Earlier in his career, Trutanich was a litigator in private practice and a federal law clerk. “I will be honored to serve as general counsel and grateful for the opportunity to lead such a talented legal team,” Trutanich said. “It is an exciting time of growth and innovation at Fox, and I look forward to working with colleagues across the company to advance our goals.”

	Also as part of the transition, the company announced that Kristopher Jones, EVP and head of government relations, will report directly to John Nallen, president and COO of Fox Corp., effective Dec. 1.

	Fox Corp.’s brands include Fox News Media, Fox Sports, Tubi Media Group, Fox Entertainment and Fox Television Stations.

	Pictured above: Adam Ciongoli (left), Nick Trutanich

schema.headline: Fox Corp. Top Lawyer Adam Ciongoli Is Exiting, Nick Trutanich to Take Over as General Counsel

title: Elizabeth Holmes Exposé Book ‘Bad Blood’ Returns to Bestseller Lists Following Nathan Fielder Doc
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Eight yea
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Eight years after its publication, John Carreyrou’s “Bad Blood” is getting another moment in the spotlight — this time courtesy of Nathan Fielder.

	The Wall Street Journal reporter’s bestselling exposé of Elizabeth Holmes and her fraudulent blood-testing startup Theranos has climbed back up Amazon’s book charts following the release of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s buzzy new documentary about the disgraced Silicon Valley founder.
	

	As of Monday, the 2018 book ranks No. 1 in three of Amazon’s bestseller categories — biomedical engineering, business infrastructure and venture capital — and No. 3,048 among all books on the retailer’s website.


		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										NO. 1 BESTSELLER						

					Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup		

		
	

	The renewed interest comes amid a huge theatrical debut for “You Can See Everything,” which opened nationwide on Oct. 16 and earned $15 million domestically over its first weekend. The nearly three-hour A24 release, filmed largely in secret, follows Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their two children during the final weeks before Holmes reported to federal prison in May 2023.

	Published in 2018, “Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup” remains the definitive account of Theranos’ rise and collapse. Carreyrou, whose reporting for The Wall Street Journal first exposed serious problems with the company’s technology in 2015, traces how Holmes convinced some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful investors that she had developed a revolutionary blood-testing machine capable of running hundreds of tests using just a few drops of blood.

	Of course, the technology never worked as advertised. By the time Theranos dissolved in 2018, its onetime $9 billion valuation had evaporated, Holmes had become the face of Silicon Valley excess, and Carreyrou’s investigation had helped turn one of the tech industry’s most celebrated startups into one of its biggest scandals.
	

	“Bad Blood” became a No. 1 New York Times bestseller following its release and spent more than 100 weeks across the newspaper’s bestseller lists. Carreyrou himself has praised the documentary, suggesting that Fielder and Oppenheim’s approach deserves Oscar recognition.

	Holmes was convicted in 2022 of four counts of wire fraud and conspiracy related to Theranos and subsequently sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. She has continued to maintain her innocence, a position that becomes a recurring point of tension in the new film.

schema.headline: Elizabeth Holmes Exposé Book ‘Bad Blood’ Returns to Bestseller Lists Following Nathan Fielder Doc

title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Screenwriter on Book-to-Screen Changes and Why Jane Austen Is So Adaptable: ‘She’s Almost Like Shakespeare’
description:
Diana Reid has more to say about “Sense and Sensibility.”

	The screenwriter for Georgia Oakley’s 2026 adaptation starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Es
body:
Diana Reid has more to say about “Sense and Sensibility.”

	The screenwriter for Georgia Oakley’s 2026 adaptation starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles grew up watching the 1995 version, from screenwriter and star Emma Thompson. When she was initially pitched the idea to create her own interpretation, she wasn’t sure it could be done because of the success of the earlier adaptation. But she went back to the original text and found the heart of what she felt hadn’t been said on screen before: the love story between the Dashwood sisters.
	

	Reid, who is primarily a novelist, took on her first screenplay from that perspective. In the process of adapting Jane Austen’s 400-plus-page novel into a just-over-two hours film, there were some scenes or characters left on the cutting room floor in order to leave room for the sisters to flourish. Reid was careful to make changes with integrity, not simply because she wanted her version to be different from the 1995 film.


	“Sense and Sensibility” is now in theaters. While in Santa Fe, N.M. to be recognized as one of Variety‘s 2026 Screenwriters to Watch, Reid spoke with Variety about the book-to-screen changes, adapting a classic novel for a modern audience and why she thinks Austen is “almost like Shakespeare.”
	
		How did you approach the project?	

	I’m a huge fan of the 1995 film. I grew up watching that film. When my producer India [Flint] suggested we try “Sense and Sensibility,” my instinct was that it couldn’t be done because that film had done it perfectly. So, I went away and I reread the book and I rewatched that film, and I had to satisfy myself that I had something to say in the book that I didn’t think had been said on screen before. And I was actually surprised, to be honest, that I did find that in the book. When I reread the book, I was so struck by the extent to which it’s really a love story between two sisters. I wanted to make sure that in the film, that always the spine of the narrative was their relationship. Then, having decided that yes, I would attempt it, it was a process of really paying attention to what resonated with me in the original, the elements of the novel that just almost didn’t require any adaptation at all, that just leap off the page, and making sure that they were really prominent, and then also being honest with myself about the bits that I felt didn’t track as well for a modern audience, and then thinking about how we could massage them while still remaining true to the spirit and the themes of the novel. From that, I worked out what I wanted to change, and then that gave me a structure, and that was what we pitched to Working Title. That’s the lovely thing about basing it on a really good book. The characters are so fleshed out, so once you’ve pitched it and you have an idea for the structure, when Working Title said yes, I was able to just start at the beginning and then right to the end, and then I edited it.
	
	
		What were those keystones that you knew you weren’t changing?	

	One thing that really struck both me and my producer was the Willoughby character and the relationship he has with Marianne. It’s actually extraordinary, when you reread the book, how modern that is, and we track it pretty closely, beat for beat. It’s interesting because we have a totally different vocabulary now around those behaviors. But what he does to Marianne is so textbook. He love-bombs her and then ghosts her, and the behaviors are identical to phenomenons that we experience today. I feel like I’ve had those experiences or friends of mine have had those experiences. That was one that leapt off the page. Similarly, I think Marianne’s character in the book, she’s almost ahead of her time. She’s a character that I think tracks very easily for modern audiences because her impulsivity and her passion is something that we really respect in this day and age. And then maybe there were three things that I felt I needed to massage. One was, and again, this goes to Marianne’s character in the book. 

	I think there’s a reading of the book where it’s a tale of sensibility yielding to sense, and Marianne, who’s the passionate sister, almost gets crushed by a society that is so oppressive and rigid, and by the end you almost feel like she’s lost some of her wonderful impulsivity and passion. And in this version, I love the idea that maybe there was a way to make it more symbiotic, so that it wasn’t about sensibility yielding; it was more about achieving a balance between the two. I just thought that was such a lovely, elegant structure, if you could set up this antithesis of sense and sensibility, and then have them combine by the end, or have them synthesize. That was another change, Elinor learning from Marianne as well, and then both coming of age at the same time. And then the final thing was there are just some features of the original plot that are hard to square with modern morals. The main one being that Colonel Brandon, in the book, is 35 and Marianne is 16, and he has a daughter who’s the same age as her, which I find as a modern reader that’s a hard hurdle to get over in terms of investing in that romance because he’s such an explicitly paternal figure. We did make some changes to his backstory to try to keep what was important about that, which is that he’s more experienced than Marianne, and he’s seen more of the world, but deprive it of the icky paternal quality.
	
	
		You mentioned that you loved the 1995 version, which I think so many people do. Was there anything that film changed from the novel that you wanted to keep or anything they changed that you didn’t want to change?	

	That film is so phenomenal. It’s funny because they actually do make quite a few changes from the novel. I think because it’s become such a high watermark for a faithful, wonderful period adaptation, people almost forget that it is also an adaptation, and they have made changes. It’s funny when you’re working in the shadow of such a brilliant text because you do try to make everything original, and in some ways that was a helpful constraint. When we were working on the film, we were always thinking, “How can we liberate it from what people have seen before?” That inspired some of the additions we made. There’s like a critical scene that we set at a party instead of a picnic because we were like, “Well, people have already seen the picnic. How can we do it differently?” But then there were some things that were unavoidable. When you condense a 400-page book into a two-hour film, there are certain things that have to be cut, and we’ve cut some of the same characters and some of the same plot beats. And I think that it’s unfortunate that they’re the same. In our film, Edward’s mother doesn’t appear, and Lucy Steele’s sister doesn’t appear, and there’s a whole sequence where Edward visits them at the cottage, which doesn’t appear in either film. You try to keep it all different. But then when you’re going through the book, you’re like, “Ah, Emma Thompson was right. That scene isn’t necessary, and I’m not going to put it in just for the sake of being different, when it objectively just isn’t necessary, or that character’s not doing anything.”
	
		The fact that Edward doesn’t visit the cottage is a really effective change, to have him just write and say, “I’m no longer coming to visit,” but it hurts every time.	

	I did a lot of work on that Edward and Elinor relationship. The way I thought about it was, in the novel, so much of the drama is her genuinely not knowing how he feels about her and her wringing her hands, being like, “What does this man want?” I think because that’s such an internal drama, it actually doesn’t play well on screen. I think what’s tense on screen is knowing that two people love each other, but that question of will they, won’t they? It’s not do they want to? It’s will circumstances conspire to keep them apart? That was how I tried to structure that Elinor-Edward relationship, like it’s clear to both of them, from the moment she gets to London, that he does love her. But it’s just a question of whether they’ll be allowed to act on that love. I just think that plays on screen so much better because it’s less dependent on internal states. It’s more about the alchemy of what’s happening between two people. Him coming to Barton and her just being like, “What do you want?” It’s amazing in a novel, but it’s just not cinematic, I don’t think.
	
	
		Are there other things that you have to change how it’s staged when you’re taking something from a book to what will play well on screen?	

	There’s a lot of that. I should say, this is the first screenplay I’ve ever written, but I’ve published three novels and I’ve written four. Got another one coming out, so I’m primarily a novelist. I think in some ways that was helpful because I’m sensitive to the benefits of both mediums. The two things I’d say: One is that in a novel, someone’s backstory can feel very compelling because you’re already having to visualize everything for yourself anyway. So, a character telling you a story that’s about something that happened in the past feels just as immediate as anything else that’s happening on the page, but in a film where you’re seeing everything, if you have a character explaining something that happened off screen, it really loses a lot of potency. In the book, there were a few things, like there was a duel that Brandon mentions happening with Willoughby, but it’s not in the action of the novel, and we put it on screen because I was like, if you don’t see it, it’s almost like it doesn’t happen in a film. And then similarly, Brandon has a whole complicated backstory that in the book he relays to Elinor, and I just felt like, as I said, in film, a character telling you about something loses a lot of potency unless you feel like it’s the person who’s telling it to is really significant. It needs to move the relationship that’s on-screen forward. So, we move that conversation so that he has it with Marianne instead of Elinor, because then it became not just about the content of the backstory, but then it’s about him being vulnerable with Marianne and her learning about him, and it’s about the progress of that relationship in the scene that you’re watching on screen.
	
		I want to talk about the ending and how we don’t really end with a wedding scene. It’s a little less structured.	

	In the book, they do both get married, but not at the same time. In the final chapter when Austen’s wrapping it all up, she says that a few years after Elinor and Edward get married, then Marianne warms to Colonel Brandon, and then they marry. This goes to what I was saying before about when you’re writing something that’s already been adapted. Austen has been endlessly adapted, not just this particular text. You are always thinking, “How can I show them something they haven’t seen before?” I think that was good because it pushed us to think about how we could end it differently. And then I came up with this idea that I liked the idea that structurally we could show how Marianne and Elinor have taken from each other because Marianne was the typical romantic, and she was the one who wanted this big romantic life, and Elinor was always the more quiet one. And then at the end, Elinor gets the textbook rom-com ending of the chase to the love of your life, and what Marianne gets is something that is still really rich, but it’s much slower and calmer. I loved that idea that the structure of the film was mimicking the way that they’ve swapped. We actually shot an additional scene, which was like a coda. It was months in the future, and Elinor and Edward were already married, and it was the morning of Brandon and Marianne’s wedding day, and it was on the beach, and it was the two couples just hanging out. It still finished on a final shot of the sisters, like it was still about their relationship, but it was to show the audience, “See, they’re all happy. They’re married, they’re paired off.” 
	

	It was one of the last things we shot. It was one of everyone’s favorite days of filming. It was a beautiful, sunny day. I’d love to see the footage. Everyone was so happy. But then we watched that scene of [Brandon] and Marianne by the river, where she sort of confesses her love to him, and their performances were just so amazing. And we just felt like the audience didn’t need another scene because you could tell from the way those two spoke to each other that they were going to be OK, and that there was such a river of compassion and love, and there was so much depth there, and that Marianne had grown up. So that’s why we ended it just after Elinor runs for Edward.
	
		What do you think it is about something like “Sense and Sensibility” that makes it possible to adapt to a modern screen but also makes it compelling? Why do you think this is possible, and people will come back to watch another adaptation of it?	

	Great art is just endlessly adaptable. I do think that Jane Austen has achieved that status where she’s almost like Shakespeare. It’s almost like she’s moved beyond being cultural property, such that I don’t feel any ownership over her, just because I’ve done one adaptation. I accept that there will be endless adaptations, and this is just my version, and someone’s probably already working on another version. I think that when characters achieve that level of cultural resonance and universality, then it opens it up to any generation and anyone who connects with the text to bring a bit of themselves to it. I just think that so few artists achieve that kind of universality. What a gift, and how incredible that no one’s trying to be definitive. Everyone’s just participating in this long chain of connected human experience with this novel that we all love. In terms of why her, like how has she got to that incredible, very rare status? I think it’s almost a unique combination of cynicism and romanticism. I think Jane Austen is so cynical about social structures and the way that people can be almost oppressed by being a social person. But then she’s so romantic about how love can be a site of agency and authenticity, and how finding someone who sees you for who you are can liberate you from those very oppressive structures, and I just think that’s a story that we’re always going to want to tell.
	

	This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

schema.headline: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Screenwriter on Book-to-Screen Changes and Why Jane Austen Is So Adaptable: ‘She’s Almost Like Shakespeare’

title: Michael Douglas Says Marvel ‘Wouldn’t Let Me’ Quit After Asking Studio for ‘Ant-Man’ Character to Be Killed Off
description: Michael Douglas reached his limit playing Hank Pym (the original Ant-Man) after two Marvel movies, but the studio refused to grant him his wish whe
body:
Michael Douglas reached his limit playing Hank Pym (the original Ant-Man) after two Marvel movies, but the studio refused to grant him his wish when he asked for the character to be killed off. The Oscar winner was asked during a recent “Happy Sad Confused” interview if the stories were true about him wanting to be killed off from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, to which he responded: “I would have been killed off after the second one, but they wouldn’t let me.”
	

	Appearing on “The View” in 2024, Douglas said he asked Marvel to kill him off in the third standalone “Ant-Man” movie, “Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania,” and even pitched an idea of how to do it that included a special effects bonanza.

	“[Getting killed off] actually was my request for the third one,” Douglas said at the time. “I said I’d like to have a serious [death], with all these great special effects. There’s got to be some fantastic way where I can shrink to an ant size and explode, whatever it is. I want to use all those effects. But that was on the last one. Now, I don’t think I’m going to show up [for a fourth].”


	Douglas debuted as Hank Pym in 2015’s “Ant-Man” and returned in three follow-up appearances: 2018’s “Ant-Man and the Wasp,” 2019’s “Avengers: Endgame” and 2023’s “Quantumania.”

	“I said, ‘I’ve never done a green screen movie,’” Douglas said on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast about wanting to join Marvel “I [told] all my agents, ‘I’d like to do one of these green screen movies to see what they’re like,’ you know? Because it’s amazing. It’s nothing, just a green screen and they show you the pictures of what it’s gonna look like when it’s all finished.”
	

	“It’s hard acting, man,” he added. “It’s coming at you here, this and that, you know… We did ‘Ant-Man’ and Paul Rudd was a wonderful actor — a lovely group — but then you can’t get out of it.” 

	Watch Douglas’ full appearance on “Happy Sad Confused” in the video below.

title: Jaafar Jackson on Playing His Uncle in ‘Michael,’ Losing the Original Third Act and the Upcoming Sequel: ‘My Job Is to Come Prepared’
description: Two years before a frame of “Michael” was shot, Jaafar Jackson wrote down a list of goals. One was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross $1 billion
body:
Two years before a frame of “Michael” was shot, Jaafar Jackson wrote down a list of goals. One was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross $1 billion at the worldwide box office.

	He did both.

	Antoine Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion worldwide and Lionsgate’s biggest release ever. It also made a star of Jackson, who had never acted professionally before.


	“I was pretty emotional,” he tells Variety. “I know how proud Michael would be of that, because he was someone who wanted to break many records.”
	

	On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Jackson opens up about leading the blockbuster “Michael,” navigating the Oscar buzz surrounding his performance and what he hopes comes next after a career-defining year.

	Listen below.

	Jackson, 30, is sitting down with Variety just two days after wrapping his second film, “Supermax,” opposite Will Smith, following 40 days of shooting in Australia. He’s candid about the life that led him here. Growing up in a house filled with 30 or 40 relatives every holiday, he dreamed of becoming a golfer, not a performer. He didn’t fully grasp the weight of his last name until he was about six, watching his father and uncles take the stage as the Jackson 5 at a reunion concert in New York and hearing the crowd erupt.

	He has fond memories of his family, especially his late uncle. One of his earliest recollections of Michael is asking him for Starbursts — specifically the pink and red ones, his favorite flavors.
	

	Bringing Michael to life, however, took two years of preparation before Jackson officially landed the role: building his own archive of songs, demos, journals, rehearsals and performances; working with acting coach Angela Gibbs; and immersing himself in the techniques of Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen. Nailing his signature voice and tone came first. After the young Jackson sent producer Graham King an unsolicited voice note speaking as Michael, he had a coach the next day. The hardest part came with learning his signature movies, particularly when performing the footwork for “Bad,” which is what closes out the film.

	But what does it mean to reenact your own family’s history? 

	Colman Domingo plays a grandfather who, Jackson says, was gentler with him than with his father, Jermaine. Nia Long, who plays his grandmother Katherine, would touch his hand in certain scenes the way his grandmother did in real life. His father Jermaine insisted on watching the film for the first time at its Berlin premiere, surrounded by an audience. And the next day, he called his son and told him, he couldn’t tell him apart from his late brother.

	Jaafar is just trying to take this all in.

	Read excerpts from his episode below.

	The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.



	

					Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson, “Michael” (Glen Wilson / Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection)
									©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		You’re here two days after wrapping a movie with Will Smith. Is that correct?	

	That’s correct. I was in Australia for about 40 days, an incredible experience, to shoot my second film and to shoot outside the country, since we shot all of “Michael” in Los Angeles. It was a whole new experience, with a new crew, a new cast and a character completely different from Michael. That excited me.
	
		So you didn’t dance or sing in this movie?	

	No, no, not at all. It’s completely different.
	
		You were born in Los Angeles in 1996. What was your childhood like growing up as a Jackson, and when did you first understand what that name meant to the world?	

	I grew up with a lot of siblings and cousins who visited on weekends and every holiday. About 30 to 40 family members were at the house, so we had lots of game nights and family cookouts, with music playing. I didn’t really realize who my family was until I was around six, when I saw them perform in New York for their 30th anniversary. Hearing the fans scream, I was scared because I didn’t understand how intense it was to see people react to someone like that.
	

	I first saw that when my dad and uncles came out on stage as the Jackson 5, and that’s the first memory I can recall of, “Oh, they’re important in some way. They have a huge fan base.”
	
		A very important follow-up. What games did you play on family game night, and how competitive does it get in the Jackson household?	

	It was always Pictionary. Boys versus girls, no doubt. It was pretty competitive, because the boys always like to brag. I think our streak was like 15 years. I think it was unfair. There are a lot more boys in the family.
	
		You started making music around 12, and your debut single, “Got Me Singing,” came out in 2019. Did you always see yourself as a musician first?	

	No. Growing up, I was only focused on golf. I started playing when I was around 4. My dad gave me golf balls to throw before I could properly swing a club, because I was so young. I fell in love with it. He got me a coach to train with once a week, then I joined a young golf club and started playing tournaments and did some charity tournaments with my father. I committed to it full time, every day, until he brought me to a recording studio and had me sit and watch him create from scratch. That shifted what I wanted to do. That was the turning point.
	
		What’s your earliest memory of your Uncle Michael? Not the icon. Just Uncle Michael.	

	Asking him for candy. He always had candy machines or stacks of candy in the movie theater, and I had a problem with an addiction to Starbursts at that age. Pink and red. I would eat too many as a kid. I remember always asking him for candy and wanting to play. He always had the latest games and game consoles, and we’d play hide-and-seek.
	
		In that house, it must have been impossible to find him.	

	He was the best at it. It was just fun, free-roaming and a blast all the time.
	
		“Michael” became the first biopic to cross $1 billion worldwide, and it’s Lionsgate’s biggest film ever. Sorry you set that bar for yourself. Do you remember where you were when you heard and who called to tell you?	

	I was at home, and I spoke with Antoine [Fuqua] and Graham King individually. We were discussing how crazy a milestone that is. Going into it, you hope and dream it’ll be that successful. I remember that two years before production even started, I wrote down a list of goals I wanted to accomplish and one was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross the $1 billion mark. When it did that, I was pretty emotional. I was proud of it, because I know how proud Michael would be. He wanted to break many records, and I couldn’t be more grateful that this did.
	
	
		I imagine you walking the earth, stalking Rami Malek. “I’m coming for your record, man.”	

	No, he’s great. I actually got to meet him in Paris during Fashion Week. He couldn’t have been nicer.
	
		Let’s talk about “Michael” Part 2. Lionsgate’s Adam Fogelson has said production could start at the end of this year or early next, with a release targeted for 2027 or ’28. Where do things officially stand? Is anything on your schedule?	

	I haven’t been told anything concrete, but whatever decision is made, I’m more than ready to get back into it and excited for where that goes. I haven’t been told a date or anything solid yet. As far as my schedule, it’s open.
	
		Leading up to the release, there was a lot of reporting about the original third act, which dealt with some sensitive subject matter. What was it like, as an actor, to lose material you had already shot and performed, knowing that footage would never see the light of day?	

	It was a massive shoot. I’ve heard many stories from other actors about how much you shoot on a project that doesn’t make it into the final picture. In the editing room, you go through scenes looking for specific performances or takes and things change constantly. So going in, I knew not everything we shot would make it into the final picture. But for me, it was the most rewarding experience because even the things that weren’t used, the experience I got from them, made me a better actor. I feel like that will happen many more times with other projects. You wish a certain performance was in there and it’s not. That’s something you have to deal with when making a film.
	
		You’re in a best actor conversation with some people like Ryan Gosling, Pedro Pascal, Matt Damon and John Malkovich. How are you approaching your first Oscar campaign? Even the movie’s detractors seem to agree: “But Jaafar is great.”	

	It’s been a crazy and surreal experience, and it’s all gone so fast. I’m taking it a day at a time. Having those conversations and being here speaking with you has been a great honor, and I’m learning so much. Whatever the studio has in mind, I’ll be there to support the film in any way I need to and I’ll be happy to do that. It’s an exciting time, and it inspires me to want to do more work and challenge myself in many different ways. To be in that conversation is definitely an honor.
	
	
		Did you know awards season was like this? That you’d have to go through all these campaign stops?	

	Not to that extent. You hear stories, but it’s a great experience to feel it and see it firsthand.
	
		What did you have to learn from scratch, and who taught you the Michael-isms and the Michael moves?	

	It started with dissecting and creating a library of footage of Michael. A library of all his songs, demos, writings and journaling, performances and rehearsals. I immersed myself in that every day. It became a full-time job, while I also worked on acting with Angela Gibbs, my head coach, who steered me in the right direction, put me in acting classes and brought in other coaches. I read books on classic teachers like Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen and studied different approaches, because there are many tools you can use, but they don’t work for every actor. I researched different ways to approach a scene, picked my favorites and then developed new ones that might work for Michael, like the dancing. It was a full immersion, a process that took about two years until I actually knew I had the role. Then it was a different energy and confidence, knowing I had it.
	
		Our chief film critic, Owen Gleiberman, wrote in his review that you got Michael’s tentative, high, sugary voice just right. Did you find the voice first or the movement first?	

	The voice came first. The movement was harder. I believe the voice was the first thing that convinced Graham because I sent him a voice note out of nowhere, over text, of me speaking as Michael. He called me and said, “Getting you a coach tomorrow.” That was the turning point.
	
		Fans keep circulating the side-by-side of your “Bad” tour rehearsal with the 1988 concert. What was the hardest move to replicate?	

	The hardest thing was feeling that true freedom on stage, so it didn’t feel rehearsed or choreographed. It’s very fluid, and that came from repetition, doing it over and over in rehearsal, so when I shot it that day, I could be completely free. I wasn’t thinking about the next move. I was present in the moment. That was the most fun part. But in rehearsal, the most challenging thing was going up on your toes, because doing it over and over hurts you. I did, many times. That move was a problem for me. I had a whole new respect for ballet dancers. Their toes are probably the strongest part of the body.
	
	
		Colman Domingo plays your grandfather, Joe Jackson. What was it like to film those scenes, knowing your own father lived through many of those tougher moments?	

	It was eye-opening to act alongside Colman, then see him as my grandfather and have that full-circle moment. It was so seamless. He’d arrive on set, I’d arrive and we’d get right into it. No rehearsals. I loved that, because we discovered things with every new take and Antoine would guide it or let us play. I grew up with a different side of my grandfather, a softer side. He was strict here and there. If you didn’t put your dishes away, he’d make sure you did or finish all your cereal. But the grandfather my father grew up with was more strict and disciplinary and wanted to keep them together as a group. It was a different time, growing up in the ’60s and parents disciplined their kids differently. Seeing how Colman channeled that, telling so much through his stillness, his eyes and the tone of his voice, was amazing to witness.
	
		Seeing it brought to life on screen would be difficult for anyone. How did it feel to be in a scene recreating something that, in theory, could be traumatic for your dad and your whole family?	

	Of course it’d be very personal, making a film about your own family and then having them watch it. I remember being really nervous about my family going to see it. I didn’t know if I wanted to sit there with them, because I didn’t want to be in my own head about what they thought of my performance. I just wanted them to enjoy it for themselves. Seeing a film about your own family can make a lot of people uncomfortable because you have your own idea of what that is, and it’s hard to capture it in a two-hour film. But the response I got from my family was incredible, and it made me emotional to get those phone calls from my cousins, even my younger cousins who are 12 and 13 and my uncles and aunts. They were so supportive, and I was happy I could bring that emotion out in them and bring them together to experience it.
	
		What did your father say when he saw the film for the first time?	

	I saw him get emotional because he first saw it at the Berlin premiere, with the crowd, with the fans. I said, “Dad, you sure you want to wait to see it there?” He said, “I’m sure.” He wanted to see it with the audience. I felt a little nervous for him, but he loved it. He had tears when he got on stage afterward. He called me later that night or the next day to say how incredible it was to see his son playing his brother and not be able to tell the difference in so many moments. I told him how high a compliment that is, if I can convince him, me being his son, that I’m actually his brother in that film. It brought back a lot of memories. He said how much he misses Michael and his smile, and that seeing me on screen brought back the presence I brought to some of those quiet moments, especially the energy in the “Bad” performance. He was incredibly proud. That’s the highest reward, to get that from your parents and your family.
	
	
		We’re at the tail end of Hispanic Heritage Month. In a clip that went viral earlier this year, you said, “I’m half Colombian and a lot of people don’t even know that.” Your mother, Alejandra, was born in Bogotá and you’ve talked about weaving Latin music into your early songs. What does being half Latino mean to you, and how have Latino audiences responded?	

	The response from the Latin audience has been amazing. I wish I’d had a chance to go down to South America or Mexico City, where I know the response to “Michael” was through the roof. As someone half Colombian, I sometimes feel embarrassed that I don’t know any Spanish. It’s not too late to learn. My mom still has a full Colombian accent, which I love. Every time I call her, I tease her about it. My Colombian side of the family is fairly small compared to my father’s side, and they’re still in Bogotá. I have some family in Mexico I don’t see often, but we keep in touch. My mom makes Colombian food every now and then. That’s a reminder, with the holidays coming up. I haven’t been to Colombia since I was 14, so I plan on going soon. The last time I was in South America was Brazil in 2019. It’s beautiful, and I love that part of the world.
	
		There are complicated feelings around this movie, about where it ends and where part two should go. As a family member who sees Michael through that lens, what’s your message to people who have their own idea of what Michael was about, including the more complicated discussions and allegations from his life?	

	Finding out who Michael was is in his music. It’s in his lyrics. It’s in the poems he wrote, the videos, the messages he put out, the talks he gave on panels and at universities. It’s in what he devoted so much time to: charities, visiting other countries and visiting countless children. Part two, I can’t say, because I don’t know. It’s not up to me. My job is to come prepared and deliver the best performance I can. But to know Michael, it starts with the music.

	10 QUESTIONS WITH JAAFAR JACKSON


Childhood nickname? Art.
Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into? Tarantulas. I have one as a pet now. And toy soldiers. I used to imagine battles with toy soldiers.
Karaoke song or shower song? I’ve never done karaoke. I’m too shy. I feel like I’d be judged completely. In the shower, I don’t have a favorite. I hum different melodies or make weird instrument sounds if there’s an echo.
Alternate title for “Michael?” It’d have to be a song title. I’m going to go with “Man in the Mirror.”
Secret talent? Juggling. 
Favorite ice cream flavor? Easily McConnell’s Sea Salt Cream & Cookies.
The one item you couldn’t live without? I can live without my phone. Maybe Apple TV, for my movies. I have a big movie collection.
What TV show or film in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of? “Troy.” Not Brad Pitt’s role, because he played that so well. Hector.
Fictional character you most relate to or admire? I’m going with Black Panther.
Favorite piece of advice you’ve received? Not to be jaded. To enjoy the most simple things in life, and that there’s beauty in front of you at all times. Just being present to look at it, not getting taken away by the illusion of what’s in front of a screen, that dopamine intake. Be present, find beauty everywhere and stay curious, with wonderment. You find happiness and joy there a lot more than in other places.


	
		Do you remember who told you that?	

	It wasn’t told to me verbally. It was through a note I found that was written by Michael. The way I found it, I felt like I was supposed to hear that.

	Enjoy the ride, man.
	

	Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more. Subscribe via Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or anywhere you download podcasts.

schema.headline: Jaafar Jackson on Playing His Uncle in ‘Michael,’ Losing the Original Third Act and the Upcoming Sequel: ‘My Job Is to Come Prepared’

            Tragedy at a Bass Pro Shops in Alabama ... a 70-year-old worker died while hanging holiday lights on the storefront's exterior.
      
    
            The Jefferson County coroner identified the man as Kurt Kralovec ... he fell from a bucket lift as he was putting up seasonal lights around the store Sunday afternoon ... according to WVTM 13.
      
    
            The Leeds Police Department is investigating the incident ... and law enforcement says it's not entirely clear how Kralovec fell from the lift.
      

            According to law enforcement radio communications, reviewed by AL.com, Kralovec plummeted 20 to 25 feet and landed on asphalt.
      
    
            Bass Pro Shops shared a statement with WBRC, saying, "Our hearts go out to the family of Kurt Kralovec, and to our entire family of Outfitters, as we grieve the loss of our dear friend and 12-year teammate. Our thoughts are with everyone affected during this difficult time."
      
    
            Police say he was pronounced dead at the scene.
      
    
            Kurt was 70.

            Hunter Schafer underwent a major gender-affirming procedure not too long ago ... revealing she had bottom surgery last year.
      
    
            She told Elle ... "I just had bottom surgery in December, which was amazing, and I love it so much."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If you're unfamiliar, bottom surgery is an operation to change a person's genitals -- often through removal and/or reconstruction -- to better align with their gender identity.
      
    
            The actress told the mag she "wanted to try to make that previous body work" because she thought the "gender-expansive" part of herself was "really cool and badass."
      
    
            But ultimately, she decided that -- while every trans person's wants and needs are different -- medically transitioning was the right move for her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hunter described a bit of the recovery period, noting she was forced to lie down a lot because her step count was severely limited.
      
    
            She said ... "I think my limit was 150 steps per day, which is nothing."

            The 63-year-old fashion designer and the much-younger stylist jetted down to Mexico before the weekend ... a little more than a month after Lori formally filed for divorce.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            While they're a couple of fashionistas, Mossimo and Hannah kept things casual as they touched down south of the border ... he wore jeans and a striped tee, while she rocked baggy pants and a gray zip-up.
      

            Mossimo and Hannah had a ton of luggage ... and he brought his golf clubs, so it looks like he'll be hitting the links at one of Cabo's finest courses.
      
    
            As we reported, Lori mentioned in her divorce filing that she and Mossimo had been separated since August 2025, but Mossimo listed their date of separation as "to be determined."
